rationale: A real corpus file (`curl/lib/cf-h1-proxy.c`) made `analyze()` die with 'Maximum call stack size exceeded' -- one crash in 900 curl files, against a lane that documents a crash guarantee of 0. The cause is C's tag/ordinary namespace split, not illegal C: the file declares `typedef enum {...} h1_tunnel_state;` and `struct h1_tunnel_state { ... h1_tunnel_state tunnel_state; ... };`, so one bare string names an enum AND a struct tag. `calculateMemorySize` resolved the member's type by BARE NAME against the struct map, found the struct, and recursed into the field list containing that field; `calculateAlignment` carried the identical unbounded recursion. This fixture is the crash guard: it fails loudly if `analyze()` throws, and it pins that all four entities are still catalogued, because 'do not crash' is only half the requirement -- the file must keep the content it could always recover. The three controls are the readings the rule must not break: a nested struct BY VALUE (legal recursion that has always worked), a pointer self-reference (the legal C idiom, never followed), and an unshadowed struct tag.
